wait/read: A recurrent network reads a text one token at a time: each step mixes its hidden state with the next token, and bends the sum with a tan-aitch.
wait/wait: So the steps stand in line: h two waits for h one, and h three for h two. A thousand tokens, a thousand steps in a row.
wait/idle: The chips that train networks do thousands of multiplications at once, in parallel, but this chain feeds them one small step at a time.
wait/blame: The tan-aitch is what holds the line. Take it out, and every state can be written straight from the inputs, all at once.
wait/history: In 2018, Eric Martin and Chris Cundy showed how to train recurrences like that in parallel along the whole sequence, making several networks up to nine times faster.
drop/one: Shrink the network to one unit, so the state and every weight are single numbers. Then drop the tan-aitch, and the bias: the old state times one weight, plus the input times another.
drop/a: Call the first weight a. It multiplies the whole state at every step, so below one, the past shrinks each time: a is the decay.
drop/b: Call the second b, the input weight, which scales each input as it arrives: a weight, not the old bias.
drop/linear: Nothing bends the sum now, just weights times numbers, added up. So it is a linear recurrence: one linear rule, recurring at every step.
drop/c: A third weight, c, the output weight, reads the state out: y t equals c times h t.
drop/h1: Say a is a half, and b and c are two. From h zero at zero, read three, one, two. Step one: half of zero, plus two times three: six.
drop/h2: Step two: half of six, plus two times one: five.
drop/h3: Step three: half of five, plus two times two: six point five.
drop/y: And y three is two times that: thirteen.
unroll/open: Now open the loop: put h two into h three, then h one, and h three becomes a sum of the inputs alone.
unroll/k: Follow one input: it enters times b, then is multiplied by a for every step it waits. The input k steps back reaches the output times c, times a to the k, times b.
unroll/bars: Here: four for the newest input, which has not waited, then two, then one. Four times two, plus two times one, plus one times three: thirteen, as before.
unroll/fade: Those are powers of a. At a half, each step back halves the weight: old inputs fade, like an echo.
unroll/move: Turn a up to one, and nothing fades. Turn it to two, and each step back doubles the weight: the state blows up.
unroll/size: So the size of a decides, written a between bars: below one, the past fades; above one, it blows up. A negative a just flips the sign at every step.
parallel/known: And here is the payoff. Those weights depend only on a, b and c, never on the inputs, so they are known before any token arrives.
parallel/rows: So each output is the inputs times those weights, added up. y two is four times one, plus two times three: ten.
parallel/all: Stack them as the rows of a matrix, and one matrix times the inputs gives every output at once: no row waits for another.
parallel/tanh: The tan-aitch network has no such shortcut: the tan-aitch bends each state before the next step uses it, so its states never become fixed weighted sums of the inputs.
